x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Unto thee, O Jehovah, do I lift up my soul.
x.Darby: [A Psalm] of David. Unto thee, Jehovah, do I lift up my soul.
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. Unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.
x.YLT: By David. Unto Thee, O Jehovah, my soul I lift up.

nt: David is speaking of his earnest prayer and worship as if he were to physically **lift up** his **soul** to Yahweh. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I pour out my heart] or [I come in prayer]

x.ASV: O my God, in thee have I trusted, Let me not be put to shame; Let not mine enemies triumph over me.
x.Darby: MyGod, I confide in thee; let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me.
x.KJV: O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me.
x.YLT: My God, in Thee I have trusted, Let me not be ashamed, Let not mine enemies exult over me.

nt: David is not using the phrase **My God** to mean that he is the only one who worships Yahweh nor that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he uses these words to emphasize that Yahweh is the God that he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You God, whom I worship,]

David is using imperative forms, **do not let me be ashamed** and **do not let my enemies exult over me**, but he intends these as polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests in your language, you could use forms that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please do not let me have shame; please do not let my enemies exult over me]

x.ASV: Yea, none that wait for thee shall be put to shame: They shall be put to shame that deal treacherously without cause.
x.Darby: Yea, none that wait on thee shall be ashamed: they shall be ashamed that deal treacherously without cause.
x.KJV: Yea, let none that wait on thee be ashamed: let them be ashamed which transgress without cause.
x.YLT: Also let none waiting on Thee be ashamed, Let the treacherous dealers without cause be ashamed.

nt: By **the ones waiting on you**, David means people who trust in Yahweh and depend on him for help. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [all those who trust in you] or [all the ones trusting in you]

David is using a double negative that consists of **not** and the negative meaning contained in the word **ashamed**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [all the ones waiting on you, you will help]

x.ASV: Show me thy ways, O Jehovah; Teach me thy paths.
x.Darby: Make me to know thy ways, O Jehovah; teach me thy paths.
x.KJV: Shew me thy ways, O Lord; teach me thy paths.
x.YLT: Thy ways, O Jehovah, cause me to know, Thy paths teach Thou me.

nt: These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. If the imperative forms do not communicate polite requests for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please make me know your ways, Yahweh; please teach me your paths]

These two phrases **Make me know your ways, Yahweh** and **teach me your paths** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Make me know your ways, Yahweh, yes, teach me your paths]

David is speaking of how to live as if it were **paths** that he could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [teach me how to live according to your will] or [teach me how I should live]

x.ASV: Guide me in thy truth, and teach me; For thou art the God of my salvation; For thee do I wait all the day.
x.Darby: Make me to walk in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art theGod of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.
x.KJV: Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.
x.YLT: Cause me to tread in Thy truth, and teach me, For Thou art the God of my salvation, Near Thee I have waited all the day.

nt: David is speaking of God’s **truth** as if it were a path that he could walk on. He means that he wants God to help him live according to God’s truth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Help me to live according to your truth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **truth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Lead me according to what is true] or [Lead me by your true teaching]

The expressions **Lead me in your truth** and **teach me** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Instruct me in your truth]

The verbs **Lead** and **teach** are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. David is humbly asking God to guide and instruct him. If the imperative form does not communicate a polite request in your language, you could use a form that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please lead me in your truth and teach me]
See how you translated the similar phrase “the God of his salvation” in [24:5](../024/005.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for you are the God who saves me]

The implication is that David waits on God to help him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I continually wait for you to help me] or [I wait on you to help me all the day]

x.ASV: Remember, O Jehovah, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindness; For they have been ever of old.
x.Darby: Remember, Jehovah, thy tender mercies and thy loving-kindnesses; for they are from everlasting.
x.KJV: Remember, O Lord, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses; for they have been ever of old.
x.YLT: Remember Thy mercies, O Jehovah, And Thy kindnesses, for from the age are they.

nt: David assumes that readers will know that when he asks God to **Remember** his compassion and covenant faithfulness, he is asking God to act according to these qualities, not simply to recall them mentally. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Act according to your compassion, Yahweh, and your covenant faithfulness]

The word translated as **Remember** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please remember your compassion, Yahweh, and your covenant faithfulness]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **compassion** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Remember how you are compassionate, Yahweh, and how you are faithful to your covenant] or [Remember to be compassionate, Yahweh, and to be faithful to your covenant]

The implication is that God has always been compassionate and faithful, not just recently. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [you have acted with compassion and covenant faithfulness since ancient times]

x.ASV: Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: According to thy lovingkindness remember thou me, For thy goodness’ sake, O Jehovah.
x.Darby: Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions; according to thy loving-kindness remember thou me, for thy goodness' sake, Jehovah.
x.KJV: Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness’ sake, O Lord.
x.YLT: Sins of my youth, and my transgressions, Do not Thou remember. According to Thy kindness be mindful of me, For Thy goodness' sake, O Jehovah.

nt: David is using the possessive form to describe **sins** that were committed during his **youth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sins I committed when I was young] or [the sinful things I did in my youth]

By **according to your covenant faithfulness remember me**, David means that he wants God to remember him with favor and blessing, not with judgment. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [because of your covenant faithfulness remember me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [or the ways I have disobeyed your instructions]
See how you translated the phrase **covenant faithfulness** in the previous verse.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **goodness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the sake of the fact that you are good, Yahweh]

x.Darby: Good and upright is Jehovah; therefore will he instruct sinners in the way:
x.KJV: Good and upright is the Lord: therefore will he teach sinners in the way.

David is using **therefore** to introduce a result clause that explains what follows from Yahweh being good and upright. If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh teaches sinners the way, he is good and upright]

David is using the adjective **sinful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [sinners]

Here David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path for a person to walk on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how to live] or [how they should conduct their lives]

x.Darby: The meek will he guide in judgment, and the meek will he teach his way.

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant love** and **faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [All the paths of Yahweh are loving and faithful]

x.ASV: For thy name’s sake, O Jehovah, Pardon mine iniquity, for it is great.
x.Darby: For thy name's sake, O Jehovah, thou wilt indeed pardon mine iniquity; for it is great.
x.KJV: For thy name’s sake, O Lord, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great.
x.YLT: For Thy name's sake, O Jehovah, Thou hast pardoned mine iniquity, for it is great.

x.ASV: What man is he that feareth Jehovah? Him shall he instruct in the way that he shall choose.

nt: מִי־זֶ֣ה הָ֭⁠אִישׁ יְרֵ֣א יְהוָ֑ה י֝וֹרֶ֗⁠נּוּ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ יִבְחָֽר

David is using a rhetorical question **Who is the man fearing Yahweh?** to emphasize that God is faithful to guide those who revere him. If a speaker of your language would not use a question for this purpose, you could translate this as a statement or exclamation. Alternate translation: [The man who fears Yahweh—God will teach him in the way he is to choose]
מִי־זֶ֣ה הָ֭⁠אִישׁ יְרֵ֣א יְהוָ֑ה י֝וֹרֶ֗⁠נּוּ בְּ⁠דֶ֣רֶךְ יִבְחָֽר

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Who are the people fearing Yahweh? He will teach them in the way they are to choose]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone]

David is speaking of how a person conducts themselves as if that were **the way** or path for a person to walk on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will teach him how he should live]

x.ASV: His soul shall dwell at ease; And his seed shall inherit the land.
x.Darby: His soul shall dwell in prosperity, and his seed shall inherit the earth.
x.KJV: His soul shall dwell at ease; and his seed shall inherit the earth.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [His soul will remain prosperous] or [He will continue to be blessed]

By **in good**, David means in prosperity or in favorable circumstances. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in prosperity]
See how you translated the term “seed” in [18:50](../018/050.md). Alternate translation: [and his descendants]

By **will inherit the earth**, David means that their descendants will continue to live in the promised land of Israel. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will inherit the land]

x.ASV: The friendship of Jehovah is with them that fear him; And he will show them his covenant.

Here, **eyes** represents David’s attention and focus. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am continually focused on Yahweh]

Here David is speaking as if his troubles were a **net** that had trapped his feet and as if Yahweh could free his feet from that trap. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Here David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a person who could physically **Turn toward** him to give attention. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to me]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because I am alone and afflicted, turn toward me and be gracious to me]
